Endow

en-DOW · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To endow gift a quality, ability, or asset.

Nature seemed to endow the youngest sister with an unusually quick wit, while her siblings had to work harder for every joke.

Worked Example

The retired opera singer used her entire estate to endow a foundation that pays for free voice lessons for children who could never otherwise afford them.

Setting up a permanent, ongoing source of support, here a foundation that will keep funding lessons for years to come, is exactly what it means to endow something.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — dow-/dot- (dos, dotare)

root — dow-/dot- (dos, dotare): a dowry; to give a dowry (Latin, via Old French endouer)

Put it together

Put it together: Endow comes from Old French endouer, rooted in Latin dos, 'a dowry' -- the property a bride traditionally brought into a marriage. To endow something is to permanently furnish it with resources, the way a dowry once permanently provided for a new household.

Use the root in a new word: dowry

Use the root in a new word: dowry: In the old story, the merchant's daughter brought a dowry of gold coins and fine silk into her marriage.

Root Check

Word Choice

Endow describes an ongoing, structural kind of giving -- setting something up so it keeps producing support long after the original gift. Compare bequeath (later in this unit), which specifically means to leave something to someone through a will, after death.
